title: Bitly
prompt: Design a URL shortener like Bitly. Users paste a long URL and receive a short URL; visiting the short URL redirects to the original. Target ~100M daily active users and ~1B URLs over the lifetime of the service.

stages.title: Functional Requirements
stages.questionPrompt: What are the core functional requirements for this system?
stages.howToAnswer: List 3-5 'Users should be able to...' statements covering the must-have behavior. Skip nice-to-haves like analytics or custom domains unless explicitly asked.

exampleHints.headline: Example (Twitter):
bullets: Users see a feed of tweets from people they follow

must: Users can submit a long URL and receive a short URL
Visiting the short URL redirects to the long URL
avoid: Drifting into analytics, dashboards, or accounts unless asked
Vague phrasing without explicit user actions

stages.sampleAnswer:
1. Users should be able to submit a long URL and receive a shortened URL.
2. Users should be able to specify an optional custom alias and/or expiration.
3. Users should be able to access the original URL by visiting the shortened URL.
hints: Two distinct actions on every URL shortener — one with the long URL, one with the short URL. Frame each as a 'Users should be able to…' statement.
Beyond the two basics, what optional behaviors might a candidate offer? Think about who picks the short code and how long it lasts.
Stay focused on the URL itself. Dashboards, accounts, and analytics are nice-to-haves — only list them if the prompt asks.

stages.title: Non-Functional Requirements
stages.questionPrompt: What are the non-functional requirements for this system?
stages.howToAnswer: Cover availability vs consistency, latency targets with concrete numbers, scale (DAU/QPS/storage), and any uniqueness/durability constraints. Tie each requirement to a real product concern.

must: Short URL uniqueness
Low redirect latency with a concrete target (e.g., <100ms p99)
Availability prioritized over consistency
Quantified scale: ~100M DAU, ~1B URLs

stages.sampleAnswer:
- Short URLs must be unique.
- Redirect latency: <100ms p99.
- Availability > consistency: a brief read-after-write delay is acceptable.
- Scale: ~1B URLs lifetime, ~100M DAU, read:write ~100:1.
- Durability: a URL mapping must not be lost once written.
hints: Pick a posture in the CAP triangle. Is a brief stale read OK on this system, or must every redirect see the latest write?
Latency lives on the redirect hot path. Pin a concrete number tied to a human / SEO concern, then quantify the scale (DAU, total URLs).
Don't forget durability — what's the cost of losing a mapping? And note the read:write skew so your caching decisions later make sense.

stages.title: Core Entities
stages.questionPrompt: What are the core entities of this system?
stages.howToAnswer: List the nouns. Don't define schemas yet — that comes in High-Level Design.

must: URL mapping (short code ↔ long URL)
should: Click event (if analytics are in scope)
avoid: Inventing entities the requirements don't justify

stages.sampleAnswer:
- URLMapping: shortCode → longURL, with optional expiration.
- (Optional) User: owns mappings if accounts are in scope.
hints: What's the smallest set of nouns that satisfies your functional requirements? You may only need one.
Resist adding entities for features not in scope — no Click events without analytics, no User without accounts.

stages.title: API
stages.howToAnswer: One endpoint per functional requirement. REST is the default — show method, path, request body shape, and response.

must: POST endpoint to create a short URL
GET endpoint that redirects from short URL to long URL
Returns the short URL on creation
should: Returns 301/302 with proper Location header on redirect
avoid: Putting URL details in URL path instead of body for create

hints: One endpoint per functional requirement. The redirect path is the interesting one — what HTTP status is right, and why?
POST takes the long URL in the body, not the path. What optional fields might a candidate include?
Return only what the client needs on success, and pick a status code that's correct for an idempotent re-create.

stages.title: High-Level Design
stages.questionPrompt: Sketch the high-level architecture. Walk through each endpoint.
stages.howToAnswer: Boxes and arrows: client → load balancer → API service → database. Note schema fields next to the database. Walk through both endpoints end-to-end.

must: Client / Load balancer / API service / Database
Strategy for generating unique short codes (counter, hash, or random)
Database choice with justification
should: CDN consideration for the redirect path
Schema fields on the database (shortCode PK, longUrl, createdAt, expiresAt)
avoid: Skipping how short codes are generated

stages.sampleAnswer:
Client → ALB → URL Service (stateless) → Cache (Redis) → DB (key-value, e.g. DynamoDB)

Short code generation: 7-char base62 derived from a centrally-issued counter (e.g., a Redis INCR or a sharded counter service). Avoids collisions by construction.

Write path: API validates URL, allocates next counter, encodes to base62, writes mapping to DB, returns short URL.

Read path: short code → cache (hit: return). Cache miss → DB → populate cache → 302 redirect.
hints: Start with the obvious skeleton: client → LB → API → database. The interesting questions are how short codes get made, and how reads stay fast.
Three families of code generation: hash-based, counter-based, random + collision check. Pick one and argue why concurrent writes can't collide.
On the read path, where does the cache live, and what's the DB cost on a miss? Your generation choice influences the schema.

deepDives.title: Short & unique codes
deepDives.questionPrompt: How can we ensure that each shortened URL is short and unique?
deepDives.sampleAnswer: Use a centrally-issued counter (e.g., Redis INCR, or a sharded ID generator like a Snowflake-style service) and base62-encode it. 7 base62 chars → ~3.5T addressable codes, plenty of headroom over 1B. Counter approach gives uniqueness by construction — no collision retry. Hash-based has collision risk at scale and leaks ordering only marginally less than the counter; the counter wins on simplicity and write-path latency.

must: Pick a generation scheme (counter, hash, or random)
Show the math: code length × alphabet ≥ URL count
Explain how collisions are prevented or detected
should: Address the bottleneck of a centralized counter (sharding, batching)
avoid: Choosing random without addressing collision retries

hints: Estimate first — how many codes do you need over the service's lifetime? That gives a lower bound on alphabet^length.
Compare hashing, counters, and random on three axes: collision probability, write-path latency, predictability.
Whatever you pick, name the failure mode. What happens when two requests race? Is the protection a constraint, a lock, or 'impossible by construction'?

deepDives.title: Fast redirects
deepDives.questionPrompt: How can we ensure that redirects are fast (sub-100ms p99)?
deepDives.sampleAnswer: Read-through Redis cache in front of the DB; DB schema keyed by shortCode for O(1) point lookups. ~95% hit rate keeps p99 under 10ms cache-side. Use a CDN that respects Cache-Control: public, max-age=86400 on 301 responses so popular links never reach origin. For the cold tail, DynamoDB-style KV with single-digit ms reads keeps p99 within budget.

must: Identify the bottleneck (DB lookup latency)
Concrete caching layer with placement (origin or edge)
should: Quantified hit rate or latency target
avoid: Adding cache without an invalidation story
Conflating cache and CDN without specifying which

hints: Walk the read path top-to-bottom. The first lookup with no cache is your worst case — does it fit your SLO?
Caches can live in 4 places: browser, CDN, in front of the DB, in the API tier. Which buys you the most? What's the key?
What HTTP semantics let the client skip your servers entirely on subsequent visits? Think Cache-Control + 301 vs 302.

deepDives.title: Scale to 10k redirects/sec
deepDives.questionPrompt: How can your system scale to support 10k redirects (reads) per second?
deepDives.sampleAnswer: ALB and stateless API tier scale horizontally — autoscale to ~20 instances at 500 RPS each. Redis cluster (3 shards × 1 replica) handles ~100k ops/sec, well over 10k. DB sees only cache misses (~5% = 500 RPS), trivially served by a single primary + 2 replicas. CDN further offloads popular short links. Total budget gives 10× headroom for spikes.

must: Layer-by-layer capacity argument
Identify which layer the cache protects
should: Mention horizontal scaling of stateless tier
avoid: 'Just add more servers' with no numbers
Stateful API hosts that block horizontal scaling

hints: Go layer by layer — ALB, stateless API, cache, DB. Which one is the bottleneck when the rest scale freely?
How big does the cache need to be to keep the long tail off the DB? A back-of-envelope is enough.
Design for headroom — interesting traffic comes in spikes, not steady-state.
